guitar.explore.title: How it works
captions: Pluck one string and the whole guitar sings. The sound starts in the string.
A guitar is six strings over a hollow wooden box with a thin top.
A plucked string swings back and forth hundreds of times a second, but moves little air.
The string shakes the bridge, the bridge shakes the wide top, and the top pushes air.
Pressing a fret shortens the string, so it swings faster and the note rises.
110 swings every second: the open A string. Fret 12 halves it to 220.

guitar.motion.title: Standing waves
captions: Pressing a fret shortens the string. Half the length gives double the frequency, so the note is one octave higher.
A string also vibrates in whole-number patterns: harmonics n = 1, 2, 3 at f, 2f, 3f.
Wave speed depends on tension T and mass per length: f = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu). Tighter = higher.

guitar.whatif.title: What if
captions: Each fret shortens the string and raises the note by about 6 percent. Twelve frets double the frequency: one octave.
A string twice as long sounds one octave lower at every fret. That is partly why bass instruments are big.

guitar.flow.title: Follow the sound
captions: A pluck pulls the string aside and lets go. The string swings back and forth at its own frequency.
The string is too thin to push much air by itself. It shakes the bridge it is tied to instead.
The bridge shakes the thin soundboard. Its large area moves a lot of air, which makes the note loud.
Pressure waves travel through the air at 343 metres per second to your ear.

guitar.number.title: The number
captions: Frequency counts swings per second. The open A string of a guitar makes 110 of them: 110 hertz.
Fret 12 halves the string, so the note doubles to 220 Hz. The wave runs along the string at 143 m/s.
Each doubling is one octave. Two octaves above this string is the 440 Hz that orchestras tune to.
